subtitle: Make equity learning part of ordinary work. This course shows how meaningful questions, accessible practice, useful feedback and visible follow-through help a learning culture grow.
scope: For DHS leaders and staff. The practice cases develop learning routines; they do not replace the DHS-required equity curriculum, formal analysis, accommodation procedures or personnel processes. Individual IDI results and inferred orientations do not become employee records or learning scores.
introTranscript: A learning culture is built through what people can ask, practice, examine and change in everyday work. Leaders can connect equity learning to service decisions, workplace culture and employee experience without treating attendance or agreement as proof of skill. This course follows a team in this example improving a confusing service-information process. You will prepare a useful learning question, examine evidence, support participation, give practical feedback, apply the learning and review the result. One DSD is led by the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant, who provides guidance and feedback while staff build their own capability. Use practice or appropriately cleared material in practice. Work at your own pace; this course does not automatically count toward required DHS training credits.

lessons.title: Start with a meaningful work question
lessons.summary: Connect learning to a decision, assumption or experience that staff can examine, rather than filling a calendar with disconnected activity.
lessons.objective: Write a practical equity-learning question for a practice work task.
objectives: Write a practical equity-learning question for a practice work task.
Distinguish attendance, skill practice and a change in the work.
Keep optional practice separate from required curriculum and formal analysis.
takeaways: A useful question connects learning with an actual task.
Attendance does not establish a skill or an equitable result.
Required curriculum and formal analysis retain their own processes.
lessons.statement: Begin with something staff need to understand or do, and explain why it matters.

image.caption: A task question gives colleagues a clear reason to learn together.

intro.heading: Choose the question before choosing the event
intro.body:
In this example, a team plans a presentation called “Equity Awareness.” Colleagues attend, but no one knows what they are expected to examine afterward. Meanwhile, service-information emails repeatedly assume that the reader already understands a program term. The team could begin with a more usable learning question: how can we explain this next step accurately to someone encountering the service for the first time? That question makes the work, audience and practical skill visible.

This does not reduce equity to easier wording. The team should also ask who is affected by the assumption, whose perspective is absent, how the question route works and what requirements must remain accurate. A reading problem can connect to language assistance, disability access, service design and decision authority. Learning can deepen understanding of those connections without pretending that a single rewrite resolves them all.

DHS’s Equity Policy expects an equity lens in everyday work and identifies required curriculum and formal analysis responsibilities. A locally chosen practice session supports capability; it does not automatically satisfy those obligations. When a proposed action falls within the policy’s formal-analysis requirements, use the required DHS Equity Analysis or Equity Scan, or the relevant customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director. Do not label a short reflection as completed formal analysis.

Set a modest observable learning purpose. Staff might identify an unsupported assumption, compare two accurate explanations, ask an evidence question or describe which authority must resolve a proposal. Distinguish that practice from implementation: a person can demonstrate a useful skill in a practice case even though the actual service process has not changed. Likewise, attendance is an activity, not a demonstration that someone can apply the skill.

Invite learning about personal assumptions as well as practical decisions. A person may notice that their familiar communication style is not universal. That reflection has value without becoming a private-belief score or an inferred IDI label. The learning question should open examination, not demand a confession.

Write the work question, why it matters, the skill to practice and the boundary of the exercise. This small preparation helps colleagues see the substance of learning and prevents a broad event title from replacing a useful purpose.

inThisLesson: Identify a task and affected audience.
Write a question staff can examine.
lessons.keyStatement: Describe what colleagues will practice and what the exercise cannot establish.

flashcards.back: A specific question about a task, decision, assumption or experience that can be examined with relevant information.
An opportunity to read, discuss or practice. Attendance establishes participation in an activity, not an equitable result.
A specific explanation or action in practice, such as finding a missing assumption or comparing alternatives. It is not a belief or identity score.
The applicable DHS-required analysis process. A locally chosen exercise does not replace its tool or consultation requirements.

accordion.heading: Prepare a learning purpose with substance

items.title: Narrow without making equity superficial
items.body: A service-email question offers a manageable entry point. Examine the audience, burden, missing perspectives and requirements around it so the activity does not become only a grammar exercise. The team may need further analysis for the actual service proposal.

items.title: Use a purpose that staff can see
items.body: “Compare two accurate explanations for a first-time reader” is more useful than “increase awareness.” It describes practice while leaving room for uncertainty. Do not promise that the exercise will prove all readers can use the service.

items.title: Leave room for personal reflection
items.body: A colleague can examine which communication habits feel normal to them and why. They need not disclose private identity experiences, be assigned an IDI orientation or demonstrate agreement to earn access to resources. Reflection and practical application can support one another.

tabs.label: Activity
tabs.body: A record that twenty colleagues attended the practice session can answer who had an opportunity to join, within the actual records process. It cannot show whether someone recognized the unexplained program term or could rewrite it accurately. Attendance helps describe the activity and examine participation opportunities. Using it as the learning result would hide the need to inspect practice and would assign achievement to people whose work was never examined.

tabs.label: Skill
tabs.body: A participant who identifies the assumed program knowledge and prepares an accurate alternative has demonstrated something specific in that practice. The explanation matters: a shorter sentence that changes the condition is not the same skill. Examine the learner’s own reasoning and revised passage rather than the coach’s finished text. This supports useful feedback without converting one answer into a claim about the person’s overall equity capability or cultural orientation.

tabs.label: Work result
tabs.body: An actual communication change needs its relevant review and authority, followed by evidence about the task it is intended to support. A clearer practice email may prepare that work, but it has not changed a service user’s experience. Keep the distinction visible when reporting progress: reviewed practice, an authorized change and its observed effects are separate. This lets the team recognize learning while identifying what still needs action or evidence.

check.question: Which is the clearest learning purpose for the practice email problem?
check.correct: Practice identifying an assumption and comparing accurate explanations for a first-time reader, while keeping formal policy requirements separate.
wrong: Prove that everyone who attends has become equitable.
Replace required DHS analysis with a brief group reflection.
Score participants’ cultural orientations from their comments.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This purpose describes a task and an observable practice without overclaiming skill, compliance or personal development.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Attendance cannot show that every participant became equitable or learned the particular skill. A brief reflection also does not replace the required DHS formal equity analysis and its applicable tool and consultation requirements. Comments about a practice task cannot establish an individual’s cultural orientation. Use a defined practice skill and its relevant evidence while keeping attendance, formal obligations and personal assessment separate.

items.text: A colleague attends the practice discussion.
The group reads a relevant policy excerpt.
A participant identifies an unstated audience assumption.
Two explanations are compared for accuracy and usability.
An actual long-term proposal follows the required formal analysis.
The authorized communication change is reviewed for remaining barriers.

lessons.next: Next, make questions and evidence useful without turning them into judgments about people.

scenario.context: A practice leader wants to report a discussion as both completed required analysis and proof of equity skill because all staff attended.
options: Describe participation and the specific practice completed, then identify any required training or formal analysis still needed.
Keep both claims to encourage confidence.
Infer an IDI stage from each person’s response.
responses: This preserves the value of the session and the actual boundaries of the evidence.
Encouragement does not justify overstating what attendance establishes.
Individual orientation labels do not belong in employee learning records.

lessons.transfer: Draft one practice work question, one observable practice and one claim the exercise would not establish.

move.control: The purpose is specific enough to guide practice.
move.failure: A broad event title substitutes for learning evidence.
move.next: State the task, skill and formal-process boundary.

lessons.title: Make questioning a normal part of learning
lessons.summary: Examine assumptions, evidence and uncertainty respectfully. Welcome a useful question without dismissing a concern or inferring motives.
lessons.objective: Separate an observation, explanation and unanswered question in a practice case.
objectives: Separate an observation, explanation and unanswered question in a practice case.
Respond to a challenge with evidence and respectful inquiry.
Identify when a concern needs a formal route rather than a learning discussion.
takeaways: A question can expose an assumption worth examining.
Observation and explanation are different kinds of statements.
Respectful learning does not replace an actual concern process.
lessons.statement: Make it possible to question a practice without turning the conversation into a judgment of the person asking.

image.caption: Inquiry becomes useful when the team can name what it knows and what remains uncertain.

intro.heading: Treat uncertainty as something to examine
intro.body:
The practice email team says that people never read instructions. A colleague asks whether the relevant instruction appears before or after an unfamiliar link. The question does not prove why people miss the next step, but it challenges a convenient explanation. A leader can help the team examine the actual message and task rather than label the colleague difficult or accept the first explanation as fact.

Separate what was observed from what is inferred. “In the reviewed examples, people asked where to send the response” is an observation with a defined source and scope. “People are careless” is an explanation about people that the observation does not establish. “Does the message identify the response route clearly?” is a question that can be examined. This distinction supports stronger reasoning without pretending that every question will have an immediate answer.

Use a calling-in response. For example: “Let us look at where that route appears and what someone would need to know to use it.” The response moves the conversation toward evidence and the task. It does not require a person to describe a painful personal experience to make the question legitimate. Nor should one colleague be expected to explain the views of everyone who shares an identity.

Respectful inquiry includes accountability. A disagreement over an interpretation may remain a learning question, but an actual allegation or immediate service concern needs the appropriate response. MMB’s Respectful Workplace policy distinguishes respectful disagreement and normal professional supervision from disrespectful conduct, and it provides actual responsibilities for concerns. Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report all allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency complaint and investigation procedures. A facilitator who is not a manager or supervisor follows the responsibilities of their actual role; employees are strongly encouraged to report. Sexual harassment follows its applicable separate policy. Do not keep a complaint inside a practice learning activity to avoid the required route.

Leaders should also name their own uncertainty. If the team lacks information about a communication barrier, say so and identify a reasonable evidence question. Missing responses cannot be treated as agreement, and one account cannot establish the prevalence of an experience across a whole population. A useful learning culture values a corrected claim because it improves the work.

Close the discussion with what was clarified, what remains open and who can take a relevant next step. This preserves momentum without pressuring the group to reach a confident answer unsupported by evidence.

lessons.keyStatement: Ask what the available evidence supports before deciding what a question means about someone.

flashcards.back: A statement about what was actually examined, with a source and defined scope.
A proposed account of why something occurred. It needs support and may remain uncertain.
A respectful invitation to examine evidence, assumptions and possible action without shaming or assigning motives.
An actual matter that follows the relevant complaint, rights, safety or service process. Learning is not its substitute.

items.title: Ask a question that can be examined
items.body: “Where does the message explain the route?” gives the group something to inspect. “Why are people like that?” attaches a broad judgment to the audience. Reframe the issue around the task without dismissing the person’s concern.

items.title: Do not require lived-experience testimony
items.body: An evidence question can be valid without personal disclosure. A colleague can choose to share a perspective, but should not be made the spokesperson for an identity group or expected to teach others through a painful experience.

items.title: Correct a claim without blaming its author
items.body: Identify the unsupported step: the examples show requests for help, but not carelessness. Explain what more would be needed to support the conclusion. This corrects reasoning while keeping accountability for the actual task.

tabs.heading: Respond to three kinds of statements

tabs.label: A documented observation
tabs.body: The colleague can point to the location of the link and describe which instruction precedes it. That observation gives the group a passage to examine, unlike saying that people never read. The source and scope still matter: one example does not establish a pattern across all service users. Starting with observable material makes the discussion more useful because another person can inspect the same instruction and offer a different explanation.

tabs.label: A proposed explanation
tabs.body: Carelessness is one possible interpretation, not a fact established by an unanswered message. An unfamiliar term, an unclear condition or a problem with the response route may also explain what occurred. Examine those possibilities without assigning a motive or asking a colleague to speak for an entire community. The consequence is a better work question: what information supports this explanation, and which part of the message or route should be examined next?

tabs.label: An actual concern
tabs.body: An actual protected-class harassment or discrimination concern is not another hypothesis for the learning group to resolve. If the facilitator is a manager or supervisor, Policy 1436 requires immediate reporting of allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and compliance with agency procedures. A facilitator without that role follows their applicable responsibilities; employees are strongly encouraged to report. Group agreement or a productive discussion does not replace the relevant response.

check.question: A colleague questions the claim that service users are careless. What is the best response?
check.correct: Inspect the message and available observations, distinguish explanation from evidence, and identify the next question without judging motives.
wrong: Treat the question as resistance to equity learning.
Ask the colleague to speak for their whole community.
Declare that the question proves the message caused every problem.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Respectful inquiry improves the claim without requiring disclosure or jumping to a causal conclusion.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling the colleague resistant assigns a motive rather than examining their question. Asking them to speak for a community substitutes identity for relevant evidence and can impose an unwanted representative role. Treating the question as proof that the message caused every problem overstates both scope and causation. Inspect the actual passage and available observations, then examine plausible explanations without deciding more than the information supports.

items.text: Reviewed examples include requests for the response address.
The message places the address after an unfamiliar link.
People miss the route because they do not care.
The placement may make the route difficult to find.
Can a first-time reader locate the response route?
An actual harassment concern uses its applicable process.

lessons.next: Next, build participation that does not depend on one format, identity or personal disclosure.

scenario.context: An actual protected-class workplace concern is raised during the practice learning session. The facilitator, who is also a manager, proposes keeping it inside the exercise.
options: Acknowledge the concern and support the relevant actual route without requiring public details; continue practice with practice material.
Require the participant to describe the incident to everyone.
Declare it resolved when the group agrees on a principle.
responses: This keeps the learning activity separate from the actual concern. As a manager, the facilitator must immediately report the protected-class allegation or incident to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follow agency procedures; no public disclosure or group resolution is a prerequisite.
Public disclosure is not the price of being heard and may expose protected information.
Group agreement cannot resolve an actual concern or replace its process.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite a practice blame statement as an observation, a possible explanation and a question to examine.

move.control: The group distinguishes what is known from what is inferred.
move.failure: Questions are treated as disloyalty or proof of motives.
move.next: Invite evidence, identify limits and preserve actual concern routes.

lessons.title: Make learning accessible and participation meaningful
lessons.summary: Design materials, timing and contribution routes so learning does not depend on a single preferred format or personal disclosure.
lessons.objective: Identify participation barriers in a practice learning activity.
objectives: Identify participation barriers in a practice learning activity.
Prepare distinct access and contribution routes without promising one format meets every need.
Avoid making identity or personal disclosure a condition of meaningful participation.
takeaways: Access is part of planning, not an afterthought.
Different ways to contribute can support the same learning purpose.
A colleague does not represent an entire group.
lessons.statement: A person should be able to practice the skill without first fitting the facilitator’s preferred way of participating.

image.caption: A well-prepared learning activity offers usable material and a clear contribution path.

intro.heading: Examine the design of the activity itself
intro.body:
The practice team plans to review the service email by displaying an image of it, asking for rapid spoken reactions and recording the discussion. That design favors people who can read the projected image, process it quickly and speak in front of the group. It may also invite unplanned disclosure. The leader should examine the learning design before interpreting quiet participation as a lack of interest.

Start with the purpose. If colleagues are practicing how to identify an audience assumption, they can inspect accessible text, consider it at a reasonable pace and contribute through an appropriate spoken or written route. Those choices can support the same skill. They do not mean every accommodation is identical or that a facilitator can settle an actual request without the relevant process. Use the current workplace accommodation and accessibility routes where applicable.

MMB’s development guidance emphasizes equal access to training and development for employees with disabilities and the possible need for reasonable accommodation. Minnesota’s ICT standard applies within its stated scope, including internal information and tools. A scanned image, a visually attractive slide or a downloaded document is not automatically accessible. Applicable standards and actual testing still matter; a general learning checklist does not certify compliance.

Prepare clear information about the activity, the relevant material and how participants can seek support through the actual route. Avoid requiring a public explanation of a disability, personal experience or identity to obtain help. Likewise, do not assign colleagues to teach or represent a community merely because of their identity. A person may offer a perspective voluntarily; the group should not treat it as a complete account of everyone’s experience.

Consider contribution and authority separately. Offering a written response does not establish that the response will influence a decision. Explain what the exercise is for, how suggestions will be considered and which matters require another role. If the team is learning on a practice case, say so. If an actual proposal is being developed, its engagement and approval requirements remain.

Finally, plan what will be recorded and shared. A session does not need a permanent record of every personal reflection. Use the appropriate privacy and records process for actual material, and make learning notes about the task rather than inferred beliefs. Access, meaningful participation and responsible information handling strengthen the activity together.

inThisLesson: Inspect the learning format for barriers.
Connect contribution routes to the purpose.
Use actual accommodation and ICT processes.
lessons.keyStatement: Plan access and contribution before interpreting a person’s participation.

flashcards.back: The ability to use the relevant material, tool and activity. A preferred format does not prove access for every participant.
A practical way to offer an answer, question or suggestion suited to the learning purpose.
Treating one person as a spokesperson for everyone who shares an identity. It can burden the person and distort the evidence.
The actual applicable process for an individual request. A learning facilitator should not invent or replace it.

items.title: Give people something usable to inspect
items.body: A screen image may preserve the email’s appearance but omit readable text structure. Prepare accessible material and check the relevant tool and export. A second file is useful only if it works for the task; calling it an alternative does not prove that it does.

items.title: Offer more than rapid public response
items.body: A reasonable opportunity to read and an appropriate written contribution can reveal thoughtful analysis that a fast round misses. Keep the purpose stable so the routes support the same practice rather than creating unrelated tasks.

items.title: Explain the limits of influence
items.body: Tell participants whether their ideas are practice answers, input into an actual proposal or something else. A contribution is not consent, and consultation does not automatically grant final decision authority. Close the loop on how actual input was considered.

tabs.label: Can the person use it?
tabs.body: A projected image may look clear to the leader while making the actual text unavailable through a participant’s reading method. Examine the relevant material and activity through the applicable accessibility process. In this case, prepared accessible text can support the same analysis question without making a colleague publicly explain a disability. That preparation does not establish full compliance or settle an individual request; it makes the design itself something the leader can improve and verify.

tabs.label: Can the person contribute?
tabs.body: Rapid spoken reactions are only one contribution method. A participant may need time to inspect the qualifying condition or may prefer to provide a considered written observation. An appropriate route can reveal reasoning the original discussion did not capture. Do not interpret silence as agreement, indifference or an orientation. The purpose is to examine the task through usable opportunities, while retaining actual accommodation responsibilities and avoiding a promise that one alternative suits everyone.

tabs.label: How will input be used?
tabs.body: A person can successfully submit a response without knowing whether it will be considered. Explain whether the email is a practice or an actual proposal, who considers suggestions and what remains outside the exercise’s authority. For example, a useful suggestion may inform a later draft without being immediately published. Clear follow-through prevents an invitation to contribute from being mistaken for a decision commitment and preserves the actual review process.

check.question: A colleague contributes little during a rapid, image-only discussion. What should the leader examine first?
check.correct: The activity’s material, pace and contribution routes, without inferring interest, ability or a cultural orientation.
wrong: Which IDI stage their participation suggests.
Whether their identity means they should have explained the issue.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The design can shape participation. Examine it and use actual support processes rather than labeling the person.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Quiet participation does not show agreement; the person may not have been able to inspect the image or contribute at that pace. It also cannot establish an IDI orientation, which is not measured by this activity. Expecting an explanation because of the person’s identity assigns a representative burden instead of examining the design. Review the material and contribution routes, and retain the actual support processes without demanding public disclosure.

items.text: Can the digital text be used with the relevant assistive technology?
How can an individual request support through the actual route?
Can staff provide a thoughtful written response?
How will actual suggestions be considered?
Silence is not recorded as agreement.
A colleague is not assigned to represent an identity group.

lessons.next: Next, use feedback to strengthen a skill without turning learning into a personal score.

scenario.context: The practice leader asks a colleague to explain all disability perspectives and record their personal story as part of the session.
options: Use appropriately prepared material and varied contribution routes; invite voluntary perspectives without making the colleague a representative or requiring disclosure.
Require the story because it will make the session memorable.
Treat refusal as failure to participate in equity.
responses: This supports learning while avoiding an identity-based teaching burden and unnecessary personal records.
A memorable story does not justify compelled disclosure or universal representation.
A person can engage in the work without providing private experience.

lessons.transfer: Redesign the practice image-only exercise with usable material, a contribution route, a support question and a clear explanation of how input will be used.

move.control: Access and participation are planned around the learning purpose.
move.failure: A single format is mistaken for equal opportunity.
move.next: Check the material, actual support route and contribution options.

lessons.title: Give feedback that develops an equity skill
lessons.summary: Explain a specific strength, an unsupported step and a useful next practice. Keep the focus on the work rather than character or agreement.
lessons.objective: Write task-specific feedback on a practice equity practice.
objectives: Write task-specific feedback on a practice equity practice.
Distinguish a supported observation from a judgment about character.
Prepare a second practice opportunity that addresses the identified gap.
takeaways: Specific feedback shows which reasoning to retain or improve.
A learning response is not an employee belief or orientation score.
A second attempt can show whether the particular skill became clearer.
lessons.statement: Useful feedback explains what to do differently and why, while recognizing what the person already did well.

image.caption: Comparing two drafts can make an improvement visible without labeling the author.

intro.heading: Move from a broad judgment to a useful next attempt
intro.body:
In this example, a colleague rewrites the service email with shorter sentences but removes the condition that explains when the step applies. “Good work” recognizes effort but gives no guidance about the missing meaning. “You do not understand equity” judges the person and still leaves the task unclear. Better feedback identifies both parts: the revised route is easier to find, but the qualifying condition must be restored accurately before the message can be used.

Focus on observable reasoning and the task’s requirements. Describe the specific passage, explain its consequence and ask the colleague to make another attempt. The consequence here is not a proven denial of services; it is that the draft no longer conveys the source’s relevant condition. Preserve that distinction. Feedback can be clear without exaggerating harm or inferring motives.

Invite the colleague’s explanation. They may have removed the condition because they thought plain language meant omitting complex material. The conversation can clarify that easier wording should preserve important meaning. This is a chance to teach the skill rather than merely mark the answer wrong. It also reveals a learning need that the facilitator’s original instruction may have contributed to.

Give another practice opportunity with enough support. Ask the person to restate the condition faithfully and explain how a first-time reader can find the response route. A worked practice example or relevant source can help. The coach should not complete every task for the learner; staff need room to reason, try and receive feedback. The One DSD consultant can provide guidance and knowledge without becoming the person who does all equity work.

Keep records and claims appropriate. A practice answer can show that a specific skill needs further work. It cannot establish a person’s values, cultural orientation or general competence. Actual performance expectations and personnel records follow their own applicable processes; do not create a hidden equity ranking from learning comments.

Close with the strength to retain, the gap to address and the next opportunity. The goal is a clearer skill and stronger work, not public praise, shame or a demand that every participant express the same opinion.

inThisLesson: Explain the gap and consequence accurately.
lessons.keyStatement: Feedback should make the next practice clearer, not create a personal label.

flashcards.back: A statement about an identifiable part of the work, what it does and how it can improve.
A useful feature of the attempt that should remain, such as a clearly stated response route.
A particular knowledge or skill that needs practice. It is not a judgment of the person’s identity or values.
Another opportunity to apply the feedback, with appropriate support and a clear purpose.

items.title: Identify both strength and gap
items.body: The practice draft improves the visible response route while losing a condition. Naming both prevents the learner from undoing the useful change or believing that a friendly response certifies the whole draft.

items.title: Explain rather than repeat the right answer
items.body: “Keep the condition” is an instruction; explaining that it defines when the step applies gives a reason. Ask the learner to restate that meaning so the next attempt practices understanding rather than memorizing the coach’s sentence.

items.title: Use support without taking over
items.body: A relevant source or worked example can clarify the task. Let the learner produce the next explanation and discuss it. Replacing their entire draft may solve a deadline problem but does not demonstrate that they developed the skill.

tabs.label: Too vague
tabs.body: “Be more equitable” names a broad aspiration but does not tell the practice learner which meaning was lost or what to retain. They might shorten the email again and remove another condition. Identify the passage and explain why the condition matters to the reader’s next step. Specific feedback turns a vague judgment into a learnable task without guaranteeing that the next attempt will be correct.

tabs.label: Too personal
tabs.body: “You are resistant” assigns a motive from a draft and can move the conversation away from the actual error. The learner may have misunderstood plain language as permission to omit complex meaning. Ask about the reasoning and examine the answer instead of labeling character or cultural orientation. This allows a clear correction of the work while keeping the explanation open to evidence and preserving appropriate personnel processes.

tabs.label: Useful and specific
tabs.body: “The route is clearer. Restore the condition that determines when the step applies, then explain how the reader can use both” identifies a strength and a gap. The learner has something useful to retain and a specific next attempt to make. A coach can model the distinction on another practice passage, then let the learner do the work. The resulting answer provides better evidence of the particular skill than praise, agreement or the coach’s rewrite.

check.question: Which feedback best supports the practice learner?
check.correct: Identify the clearer route, explain the lost condition, invite the reasoning and ask for a faithful second attempt.
wrong: Tell them their cultural orientation caused the error.
Praise effort and approve the draft without checking the condition.
Rewrite everything for them and report the skill as mastered.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The feedback preserves the strength, teaches the gap and provides another opportunity without claiming more than the practice shows.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A draft error cannot identify the learner’s cultural orientation. Praise without restoring the qualifying condition can approve a message whose meaning is incomplete. Rewriting everything for the person produces the coach’s answer, not evidence that the learner has mastered the skill. Identify the strength and missing meaning, invite the reasoning and support the learner’s own second attempt.

items.text: The response address is easier to locate in this draft.
The revised sentence omits the relevant condition.
Restate the condition using the verified source.
Explain how the reader knows when the step applies.
This answer proves the person has reached Adaptation.
The missing condition proves the learner does not care.

lessons.next: Next, connect the practiced skill with an actual work decision through the appropriate process.

scenario.context: A practice coach corrects every sentence and wants to record the learner as having mastered the skill.
scenario.prompt: What would better support the learning claim?
options: Have the learner make and explain a second practice attempt using the feedback, then describe only what that attempt shows.
Use the coach’s finished draft as proof of the learner’s skill.
Assign a general equity rating from their willingness to accept changes.
responses: The learner’s own attempt supplies relevant evidence of the particular skill.
A coach’s work shows the coach’s contribution, not the learner’s independent ability.
Agreement is not a valid measure of equity skill or cultural orientation.

lessons.transfer: Write feedback on a practice draft using one strength, one specific gap, a consequence and a second practice task.

move.control: The feedback gives a clear next attempt.
move.failure: A broad compliment or personal judgment replaces teaching.
move.next: Describe the work and let the learner apply the guidance.

lessons.title: Carry learning into the actual work
lessons.summary: Connect a practiced skill with a feasible next step, responsible roles and the applicable decision process. Avoid treating practice as permission to change a service.
lessons.objective: Identify a realistic transfer step from a practice skill to a work task.
objectives: Identify a realistic transfer step from a practice skill to a work task.
Separate staff preparation, consultant support and actual decision authority.
Recognize when a proposed change needs a formal analysis or specialist process.
takeaways: A skill needs an appropriate opportunity for use.
Learning does not grant authority to change a policy or service.
Consultant support develops staff capability rather than replacing staff work.
lessons.statement: Turn the learning into a clear next task, with the relevant requirements and authority visible.

image.caption: A transfer plan connects learning with who can prepare, review and decide.

intro.heading: Prepare the next step without skipping the real process
intro.body:
The practice team has practiced writing a clearer service email. A staff member wants to replace the actual message immediately. The learning has value, but the draft still needs the relevant subject-matter, publication and service review. If the communication is part of a long-term proposal, the applicable DHS formal equity analysis also remains. A practice answer is preparation for work, not permission to change it.

Choose a transfer step that the person can reasonably take. They might prepare a draft, identify the current source, map the response route or ask the responsible role to clarify a condition. That step should fit their role, available time and the actual process. “Improve everything” is too broad to guide follow-through and can leave the staff member responsible for decisions they cannot make.

Separate responsibilities. Staff examine their work and prepare relevant information. The One DSD Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and can provide guidance, leadership, knowledge and feedback. A subject-matter role verifies content within its area. Actual decision, publication, privacy, accessibility and policy responsibilities follow the applicable process. Do not treat consultant guidance as replacing a formal departmental role or required equity-director consultation.

Consider which learning connections help now. The email task may benefit from plain language, language-access planning, accessible documents and equity analysis. Offer the relevant resource at the point it supports the task rather than making people complete every course before they can work. The program is an integrated resource for capability, not a set of artificial access gates.

Make the transfer visible with a short planning note: the task, the skill to apply, the relevant source or requirement, who prepares it, who resolves the decision, and how the next step will be reviewed. Record an unresolved requirement as unresolved. A planned date is not proof the authority, resources or review are available.

If an actual concern needs immediate attention, use the appropriate route rather than waiting for the learning plan. Transfer should strengthen responsible work. It should not delay a service need, create an unapproved commitment or imply that the person must become an expert before raising a valid question.

inThisLesson: Identify the actual authority and source.
Keep formal requirements and urgent routes active.
lessons.keyStatement: Practice prepares a next step; the real work still follows its actual responsibilities.

flashcards.back: A feasible task that uses a practiced skill in the relevant work, with its requirements and authority identified.
The actual role or process that can authorize a change. Participation in learning does not create it.
Guidance, leadership, knowledge and feedback that help staff build their own capability.
Relevant learning or a tool offered where it helps the current task, without an unnecessary completion gate.

items.title: Choose a task inside the person’s role
items.body: Preparing a source-grounded draft may be feasible even when changing a service is not. Identify the boundary so the person can make a contribution without inheriting a decision they cannot authorize.

items.title: Do not confuse support with formal sign-off
items.body: The consultant’s feedback can strengthen the analysis. The actual proposal still follows the required departmental tools, consultation and decision processes. Naming that distinction protects the contribution instead of overstating its authority.

items.title: Connect resources to the question
items.body: A plain-language resource helps preserve meaning; language-access guidance helps examine a help route; accessibility guidance helps review the artifact. These are connected aspects of the same task rather than competing programs. Choose what supports the current work.

tabs.heading: Three responsibilities in a transfer step

tabs.label: Prepare
tabs.body: A staff member can locate the current service instruction, identify the audience assumption and prepare a source-grounded question or draft. That preparation gives the person responsible something concrete to examine, even if the staff member cannot authorize publication. A useful next task fits the person’s role and available support. It is more workable than assigning responsibility to improve every message or treating a planned date as proof that approval and resources exist.

tabs.label: Support
tabs.body: The consultant can explain an equity consideration, offer a relevant example and give feedback on the staff member’s reasoning. A subject-matter specialist can verify the condition within their actual role. Those contributions strengthen preparation without replacing the staff member’s own work or granting blanket permission to act. The practice team should retain feasible tasks so that guidance develops capability rather than becoming permanent substitution.

tabs.label: Decide and follow through
tabs.body: The actual decision process determines whether and how the proposed email change can proceed. Content, service, privacy, accessibility and publication responsibilities may need attention, with formal equity analysis where required. After an authorized change, someone must still examine its implementation and relevant effects. Identifying these responsibilities prevents a correct practice answer from being treated as an approved communication or a demonstrated service improvement.

check.question: A participant has a strong practice rewrite. What is an appropriate next step for the actual service email?
check.correct: Prepare the actual source-grounded draft and route it through the relevant content, access and decision processes, including formal analysis where required.
wrong: Publish it immediately because the practice answer was correct.
Ask the consultant to do every remaining task for the team.
Block all resource access until every staff member completes all courses.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This uses the skill while retaining the real process and the staff member’s responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A correct practice rewrite does not authorize immediate publication of an actual service message. Giving every task to the consultant avoids the staff practice and responsibility the program is meant to develop. Requiring every course before any resource can be used creates an unrelated learning gate rather than supporting the immediate task. Prepare the relevant draft and use actual support, analysis and decision processes.

scenario.context: The practice leader gives the consultant all equity tasks because staff have only just begun learning.
options: Give staff feasible preparation tasks and relevant support, while the actual decision process retains its authority and requirements.
Keep all work with the consultant indefinitely.
Let staff bypass requirements to prove independence.
responses: Staff capability grows through supported practice and real responsibility, with the proper boundaries retained.
Permanent substitution prevents staff from building the intended capability.
Independence does not mean skipping a required process or acting outside authority.

move.control: A feasible next task connects learning to work.
move.failure: Practice is mistaken for permission or staff work is handed away.

lessons.title: Review whether the learning is helping
lessons.summary: Use specific practice and work evidence, keep missing information visible, and improve the learning design without creating personal equity rankings.
lessons.objective: Choose evidence suited to a learning activity, skill or work result.
objectives: Choose evidence suited to a learning activity, skill or work result.
Write a limited conclusion from practice follow-up information.
Identify a useful adjustment without inferring personal orientation or causation.
takeaways: The evidence must fit the question being asked.
Review should improve learning and work rather than rank people’s identities or beliefs.
lessons.statement: Describe what changed, what the evidence supports and what still needs examination.

image.caption: A useful review keeps activity, demonstrated practice and actual work results separate.

intro.heading: Make progress visible without overstating it
intro.body:
The practice team reports that twenty colleagues attended a session and five revised drafts were reviewed. That information shows activity and available practice material. It does not show whether every colleague developed the skill or whether service users can now understand the actual email. A useful review asks the right question at each point instead of using the easiest count as the answer to everything.

For activity, describe what occurred and who had an opportunity to participate through the appropriate records. For practice, examine specific work: did the revised draft preserve the condition and make the response route clear? For the actual service communication, use the appropriate review and relevant evidence about the task. These are different forms of information with different limits.

Missing information matters. If no follow-up was collected from a particular route or the actual message has not been changed, say so. No response is not evidence that the learning worked or that there are no barriers. A report can accurately recognize useful preparation while keeping unresolved questions visible.

Do not infer causation from a small before-and-after observation. Fewer requests for help could reflect a clearer message, a different audience, a changed reporting route or other conditions. Compare the source, definition, period and context before describing a pattern. If the information cannot support a conclusion about who is affected, do not fill the gap with a stereotype or an invented estimate.

Review the learning design too. Staff may need a better worked example, more time with the source, accessible material or clearer feedback. That adjustment is a leadership task, not proof that colleagues lack commitment. Recognize useful questions and corrections because they make the work stronger. Keep personal reflections and individual IDI information out of employee rankings or hidden scores.

Close the loop with a practical summary: what was done, which skill was demonstrated in the reviewed examples, what work has changed, what remains uncertain and what the next review will examine. This gives learning substance while preserving the difference between a promising practice and a demonstrated result.

inThisLesson: Adjust the activity and next work step.
lessons.keyStatement: A credible learning review makes its evidence and limits as clear as its accomplishments.

flashcards.back: Information about what learning occurred. It does not establish skill or impact by itself.
Specific work from an exercise that can support a limited conclusion about a skill.
Relevant information about an actual task or result, examined with its source, definition and limitations.
A question the available information cannot answer. Missing follow-up is not a favorable result.

items.title: Report the denominator of the claim
items.body: If five drafts were reviewed, say what those five show rather than extending the conclusion to everyone who attended. The group may use that information to improve teaching, but it cannot treat a limited sample as a complete skill assessment.

items.title: Separate a pattern from its cause
items.body: An observed change can justify another question. It does not automatically prove that the session caused the change. Examine relevant differences in the task and information before deciding what the pattern means.

items.title: Use the review to improve conditions
items.body: If people omit the same condition, revisit the example, instruction and feedback as well as the attempts. A learning culture takes responsibility for how the skill is taught instead of converting repeated confusion into a character judgment.

tabs.label: Supported
tabs.body: The reviewed practice drafts now retain the condition and show the response route. That is a useful, bounded result because it describes actual material examined against a specific skill. It does not establish what unreviewed participants can do or how an actual recipient experiences the published email. Report the improvement precisely so that genuine learning is visible without expanding the conclusion beyond the evidence.

tabs.label: Still open
tabs.body: The actual message has not completed its review, and relevant service follow-up is missing. Those are unanswered questions, not evidence of failure or success. Acknowledging them helps the team choose the next investigation rather than filling the gap with a reassuring story. The report can recognize improved practice and still say that the service effect is unknown; both statements can be accurate at the same time.

tabs.label: Next step
tabs.body: The team can prepare the actual review, improve the worked example and identify what evidence would help examine the response route. Each is a next task with its own purpose and actual authority. A future review date is a plan rather than a result. Explain what the next step will examine and retain uncertainty about its outcome, instead of describing a hoped-for reduction in barriers as already achieved.

check.question: Which conclusion fits five improved practice drafts and no actual service follow-up?
check.correct: The reviewed practice improved in specific ways; the actual service effect remains unknown and needs the appropriate follow-up.
wrong: All staff have achieved intercultural competence.
The course caused a reduction in service disparities.
No follow-up means there are no remaining barriers.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The conclusion recognizes a supported improvement while keeping its scope and the missing evidence clear.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Five reviewed practice drafts cannot establish intercultural competence for every staff member. They also cannot show that the course caused a reduction in actual service disparities, which requires relevant evidence and a sound causal basis. Missing follow-up leaves barriers unknown rather than proving their absence. Report the specific practice improvement, preserve its scope and identify the service question that still needs appropriate examination.

sorting.heading: Match the reporting statement to its evidence

items.text: Five reviewed practice drafts retain the condition.
Twenty colleagues attended the activity.
How does the actual service message work after its authorized revision?
Who could not participate through the offered routes?
Attendance proves every person has developed equity skill.
Missing follow-up proves no barriers remain.

scenario.context: A practice progress report says the session eliminated a disparity, but its only evidence is attendance and several practice drafts.
options: Report the activity and specific draft improvements, remove the unsupported impact claim and identify the actual work question still needing evidence.
Keep the claim because it motivates staff.

responses: This makes genuine progress visible without substituting motivation or personal judgments for evidence.
A positive purpose does not make an unsupported claim accurate.
Personal rankings would not answer the work question and can create inappropriate records.

move.control: The conclusion fits the available information.
move.failure: Activity or missing data is presented as a proven result.
